questions.q: What did the classroom study show about the woman who attended more sessions?
a: Students preferred her without realizing they had seen her
Students rated her less attractive than the others
Students remembered her name better than the rest
Students assumed she was the course instructor
questions.why: Lesson 1 says familiarity breeds preference even when people do not consciously recognize the person.

questions.q: Why do we often adopt other people's opinions?
a: It saves us the effort of figuring things out
It makes us seem more confident to strangers
We are naturally unable to form our own views
It helps us avoid conflict with authorities
questions.why: Lesson 2 says taking on others' views saves time, and social pressure adds another push to conform.

questions.q: In the line-matching study, what made participants give a wrong answer?
a: Actors in the group had already answered incorrectly
The lines were genuinely difficult to compare
Participants were rushed by a strict time limit
The researchers gave unclear instructions
questions.why: Lesson 2 says six of seven people were actors, and a third of real participants conformed.

questions.q: How does the presence of others affect a difficult task?
a: It makes it harder, because we focus on appearing smart
It makes it easier, because we feel energized
It has no measurable effect on performance
It helps most when the audience is large
questions.why: Lesson 3 says spectators trigger fight, flee or fun responses that interfere with hard problems.

questions.q: What does the summary suggest for using social influence to your advantage?
a: Spend time with someone who is good at your goal
Work alone until you have mastered the skill
Compete against people who are weaker than you
Avoid groups that discuss their successes
questions.why: Lesson 3 advises working near the hardest worker or running with an athletic sibling.
